questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: state the condition under which the antiderivative power rule applies
questions.stem: A reference card lists the power rule for antiderivatives as x to the power n plus 1, all divided by n plus 1. Which restriction on n does that formula carry?

options.text: The exponent must be any real number other than negative one
The exponent must be a positive integer, which rules out fractional powers
options.misconception: believes the antiderivative power rule only covers integer exponents

options.text: The exponent must be a whole number other than negative one, so rational powers are excluded
options.misconception: believes rational exponents fall outside the antiderivative power rule

options.text: The exponent must be zero, since only constant integrands have elementary antiderivatives
options.misconception: believes only constant integrands can be integrated in closed form

questions.explanation: The formula is read backwards from the derivative rule: since the derivative of x to the power n plus 1 is n plus 1 times x to the power n, dividing by n plus 1 recovers x to the power n for every n other than negative one, fractional exponents included. The single excluded case is n equal to negative one, where n plus 1 is zero and the division is undefined, and that case is handled by the logarithm rule instead.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the denominator n plus 1 when the exponent is negative one.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: extract a constant multiplier from an integral
questions.stem: A sensor model integrates a fixed gain k times a pulse shape f of x, where k never changes. Which rule correctly takes the gain out of the integral?

options.text: The constant comes straight out in front as a factor on the whole integral
The constant must itself be integrated, contributing a factor of k times x
options.misconception: believes a constant inside an integral must be treated as a variable

options.text: The constant can only leave the integral when it happens to be positive
options.misconception: believes a negative constant cannot be pulled out of an integral

options.text: The constant multiplies the antiderivative but is cancelled by the variable
options.misconception: believes the constant cancels against the variable when the integral is evaluated

questions.explanation: Linearity in the integrand says that scaling the function scales the accumulated amount by the same factor, so k times the integral of f equals the integral of k times f. Nothing about the sign of k changes this, and nothing needs integrating on behalf of k because k is constant with respect to the variable of integration. Treating k as a variable is what produces the spurious factor of kx.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a total when the rate producing it is scaled.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: split the integral of a sum into a sum of integrals
questions.stem: A vibration trace combines a pulsing part and a steady drift part, and the two totals must be added together. Which statement correctly splits that combined integral?

options.text: The integral of the sum equals the sum of the two separate integrals
The integral of the sum equals the product of the two separate integrals
options.misconception: believes integrating a sum multiplies the pieces together

options.text: A sum may be split only when both parts depend on the same variable
options.misconception: believes linearity requires the terms to share a variable before it applies

options.text: The integral of the sum equals the sum divided by the number of terms
options.misconception: believes integrating a sum averages its terms instead of adding them

questions.explanation: Accumulation is additive: the total change produced by a combined rate is the total from the first part plus the total from the second, which is exactly what the sum rule states. No averaging appears, and the pieces need not share a variable as long as each is integrable over the same interval. Multiplying the parts would be right for a product rule in reverse, not for a sum.
questions.hint: Compare the physical total from a combined rate with the totals of each part alone.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: integrate a negative fractional power by substitution
questions.stem: A decay model produces an integrand of x to the power negative three halves, an exponent that is both negative and fractional. Which method genuinely evaluates it?

options.text: Substitute u equal to the square root of x, turning the integrand into a negative integer power
Apply the plain power rule with n set to negative three halves and accept the result
options.misconception: believes the power rule handles negative fractional exponents without further work

options.text: Differentiate the integrand first, then reverse that derivative to obtain the antiderivative
options.misconception: believes differentiating first automatically produces the antiderivative

options.text: Treat it as a logarithm, because a negative exponent on x signals the log case
options.misconception: believes every negative exponent must be integrated with a log rule

questions.explanation: Setting u equal to the square root of x makes x equal to u squared and dx equal to two u du, so x to the power negative three halves becomes u to the power negative three and the leftover supplies a factor of two u. What remains is two times the integral of u to the power negative two, an integer power the power rule finishes at once. The direct power-rule attempt fails because the exponent is not an integer, and logs appear only at exactly negative one.
questions.hint: Try to remove the fractional power by writing x as the square of something.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: integrate the reciprocal function on both branches of its domain
questions.stem: A records desk needs the antiderivative of one over x, and part of its data sits at negative values of x. Which expression is correct there, and why?

options.text: The natural logarithm of the absolute value of x, since its derivative is one over x
The natural logarithm of x, because that alone has derivative equal to one over x
options.misconception: believes the log antiderivative exists only where x is positive

options.text: The natural logarithm of x plus a separate constant chosen for each branch
options.misconception: believes one extra constant is needed to join the two branches of the domain

options.text: The natural logarithm of x restricted to positive x, so the sign issue disappears
options.misconception: believes avoiding the negative branch removes any need to reason about signs

questions.explanation: Differentiating the logarithm of the absolute value of x uses the chain rule with a factor of one over the absolute value times the sign of x, and the two signs combine to give one over x everywhere x is nonzero. That single expression therefore works on the positive and negative branches at once, which is why no branch-specific constant is needed. Writing the plain logarithm of x leaves the negative branch without an antiderivative.
questions.hint: Check the derivative of the log of the absolute value on a negative input.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: identify the exponential antiderivative
questions.stem: A growth law needs the antiderivative of the exponential function e to the x. Which pairing of statements about it is correct?

options.text: It is e to the x plus a constant, since that function is its own derivative
It is x times e to the x, since multiplying by the variable supplies the antiderivative
options.misconception: believes a reversed product rule replaces the exponential antiderivative

options.text: It is e to the x divided by x, because dividing by the variable removes the growth
options.misconception: believes dividing an exponential by its argument gives an antiderivative

options.text: It is the natural logarithm of e to the x, because logs invert exponentials
options.misconception: believes an antiderivative of an exponential must be the inverse function

questions.explanation: The derivative of the exponential function is the exponential function itself, so the exponential undoes itself and its antiderivative is the exponential plus a constant. Multiplying by the variable instead produces a derivative carrying an extra copy of the exponential that the integrand does not have, and dividing by the variable is not even defined at the origin. Inversion plays no part, since an antiderivative and an inverse function are different kinds of object.
questions.hint: Ask which familiar function is unchanged by differentiating itself.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: match trigonometric functions with their antiderivatives
questions.stem: A survey team is matching trigonometric functions with the antiderivatives it will need on site. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Sine pairs with negative cosine, and secant squared pairs with tangent
Sine pairs with positive cosine, and secant squared pairs with negative tangent
options.misconception: believes both standard pairs carry a sign error in the same direction

options.text: Cosine pairs with negative sine, and secant squared pairs with secant times tangent
options.misconception: believes secant squared integrates to a product of secant and tangent

options.text: Sine pairs with negative cosine, and secant squared pairs with secant itself
options.misconception: believes the antiderivative of secant squared is the secant function

questions.explanation: Each pairing is fixed by differentiating the proposed answer: the derivative of negative cosine is sine, and the derivative of tangent is secant squared, so those two are the correct partners. Secant times tangent is instead the derivative of secant, which is why it belongs to secant and not to secant squared. Sign errors are the common slip here, so each pair is worth confirming by differentiating before committing to it.
questions.hint: Differentiate each proposed answer and see which one reproduces the function.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: state the fundamental theorem in evaluation form
questions.stem: A flow total is reported as the definite integral of a rate over an interval. Which statement correctly connects that number to an accumulation function?

options.text: It is the antiderivative at the upper limit minus the same antiderivative at the lower limit
It is the antiderivative at the lower limit minus its value at the upper limit
options.misconception: believes the limits enter the evaluation in increasing order regardless of the notation

options.text: It is the integrand at the upper limit minus the integrand at the lower limit
options.misconception: believes a definite integral is a difference of function values, not antiderivative values

options.text: It is the antiderivative of the two limits, taken by reversing the differentiation
options.misconception: believes the limits are themselves differentiated rather than substituted into an antiderivative

questions.explanation: The fundamental theorem says the definite integral of a continuous function equals the net change in any of its antiderivatives between the two limits, with the upper limit entering positively. Substituting the integrand instead of an antiderivative measures a difference of heights, not accumulated area, and reversing the order of the limits reverses the orientation of the accumulation, which is the source of the sign error in the second option.
questions.hint: Think of the definite integral as net change in an accumulated quantity.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: recognise when the inner derivative required by substitution is absent
questions.stem: Two integrals wait in a queue: the integral of 2x times the quantity x squared plus 1, cubed, and the integral of that same quantity cubed on its own. Why does a single substitution finish only the first?

options.text: The first integrand already carries the inner derivative 2x, and the second has no such factor
The first integrand is a product of two pieces while the second is a single power
options.misconception: believes products and single powers need different methods as a matter of form

options.text: The first integrand has an integer exponent while the second carries a rational one
options.misconception: believes the kind of exponent decides whether substitution applies

options.text: The first integrand is continuous everywhere while the second is not
options.misconception: believes continuity decides whether a substitution can be carried out

questions.explanation: A substitution works when the leftover factor in the integrand is exactly the derivative of the inner expression, because that is what turns the new differential back into the old one. The derivative of x squared plus 1 is 2x, and the first integrand contains precisely that factor, so the rest integrates as a plain power of the new variable. The second has nothing matching that derivative, so the same substitution leaves the new variable inside the differential and no progress is made.
questions.hint: Look for the derivative of the inner expression sitting outside the power.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: choose the substitution that absorbs the leftover differential
questions.stem: A growth model requires the integral of x times e to the quantity x squared. Which choice of the new variable lets the substitution actually complete the job?

options.text: Take the new variable as x squared, so the leftover x dx becomes the new differential
Take the new variable as x itself, so the exponential becomes the new differential
options.misconception: believes the outer function should be renamed as the new variable

options.text: Take the new variable as e to the quantity x squared, treating x as a leftover constant
options.misconception: believes renaming the whole exponential factor leaves a plain power to integrate

options.text: Take the new variable as the entire product of x with e to the quantity x squared
options.misconception: believes the whole integrand can be renamed as a single new variable

questions.explanation: The new variable should be the inner expression whose derivative appears among the leftover factors. The derivative of x squared is 2x, and the integrand does contain a copy of x dx, so renaming x squared absorbs the exponential into a plain power and the remaining integral is immediate. Renaming the outer exponential instead leaves x behind, which still depends on the new variable, so nothing has been gained.
questions.hint: Pick the new variable whose derivative is hiding in the leftover factors.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: decide which factor to differentiate in integration by parts
questions.stem: An engineer must integrate the product of x and e to the x by parts. Which assignment of roles is the standard and productive one?

options.text: Take the polynomial factor as the one to differentiate and integrate the exponential factor
Take the exponential factor as the one to differentiate and integrate the polynomial factor
options.misconception: believes the role assignment is arbitrary because either order gives the same result

options.text: Take the whole product as the one to differentiate and integrate the constant multiple
options.misconception: believes the parts formula applies by differentiating the entire product

options.text: Take the constant multiple as the one to differentiate and integrate the entire sum
options.misconception: believes a constant can serve as the differentiated part of a parts formula

questions.explanation: The parts formula is u dv equals uv minus the integral of v du, so the role that gets differentiated is the one whose derivative is simpler than the original. Differentiating the polynomial x produces the constant 1, which makes the leftover integral easy, while differentiating the exponential reproduces an exponential and leaves the harder problem behind. The rule of thumb is to differentiate the algebraic or logarithmic factor and integrate the exponential or inverse-trigonometric one.
questions.hint: Ask which factor becomes simpler when you differentiate it once.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: describe the repeated reduction procedure for polynomial times exponential
questions.stem: A repeated reduction is needed for the integral of x squared times e to the x. What does the tabular procedure actually do to get there?

options.text: It differentiates the polynomial column until it vanishes, then reads off a signed diagonal sum
It integrates the polynomial column until it vanishes, then reads off a single product
options.misconception: believes the polynomial column is integrated repeatedly rather than differentiated

options.text: It substitutes a new variable equal to x squared and reduces the problem to a rational integral
options.misconception: believes the polynomial times exponential case reduces to partial fractions

options.text: It expands the exponential as an infinite series and integrates term by term
options.misconception: believes the tabular method is a disguised series expansion

questions.explanation: The tabular method runs integration by parts over and over, each time differentiating the polynomial by one degree. The derivatives x squared, x, 1 and then 0 are stacked in one column with the exponential in the other, and the alternating signs along the diagonals turn the repeated parts formula into a single sum, here giving the exponential of x times the quantity x squared minus 2x plus 2. It terminates because a polynomial eventually differentiates to zero.
questions.hint: Ask what operation is repeated until it stops producing anything.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: name the three algebraic cases of partial fraction decomposition
questions.stem: A rational function must be split into simpler pieces before it can be integrated. Which set of denominator factor types covers every case that can arise?

options.text: A repeated linear factor, a distinct linear factor, and an irreducible quadratic factor
A linear factor, a quadratic factor, and a cubic factor of any shape at all
options.misconception: believes partial fractions are classified by the total degree of the denominator

options.text: A linear factor raised to a power, a factor with no real roots, and a plain constant
options.misconception: believes a constant in the denominator is a separate decomposition case

options.text: A factor that stays positive, a factor that stays negative, and a factor vanishing at the origin
options.misconception: believes the sign of a factor rather than its root structure sets the case

questions.explanation: Over the reals a denominator factors into linear and irreducible quadratic pieces, and a real quadratic needs no splitting at all. The linear pieces are then handled by multiplicity: a distinct linear factor contributes one term, while a factor repeated to the power m contributes one term for each power from 1 up to m. Classification by total degree or by sign ignores root structure, which is the only thing that determines the shape of the split.
questions.hint: Classify factors by their real roots and by how often those roots repeat.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: write the split for a denominator with a squared linear factor
questions.stem: A rational integrand has a denominator of the quantity x minus 3, squared. What must the numerator of the correct split look like?

options.text: One constant over x minus 3, plus a second constant over the squared quantity x minus 3
A single constant over the squared quantity x minus 3, with no first-power term
options.misconception: believes a repeated factor contributes only the highest power in the split

options.text: One constant over x minus 3, plus a linear expression over the squared quantity
options.misconception: believes a repeated linear factor needs a linear polynomial in the numerator

options.text: Two constants over x minus 3, plus a further constant over the cubed quantity
options.misconception: believes the split must include a power one higher than the multiplicity

questions.explanation: The rule for a linear factor raised to the power m is to include one term for each power from 1 up to m, each with its own constant numerator. For m equal to 2 that means a first-power term and a squared term, both with constant numerators, and no cubic term appears. Omitting the first-power term loses the freedom needed to reproduce the original numerator, and adding a cubic term makes the split over-parametrised.
questions.hint: Count the powers of the factor and include one term for each of them.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: decide convergence of an improper integral by comparison
questions.stem: A detector measures an intensity that falls off like one over x squared, integrated over an unbounded interval. Which reasoning correctly settles whether the total is finite?

options.text: It is finite, because one over x squared is bounded above by one over x to the three halves power
It is infinite, because any power of x in the denominator makes the total diverge
options.misconception: believes every power-law decay over an unbounded interval diverges

options.text: It is infinite, because the integrand stays above one near the finite end
options.misconception: believes the size of the integrand near the lower limit forces divergence

options.text: It is finite, because the integrand approaches zero as x grows past every bound
options.misconception: believes an integrand tending to zero is sufficient for a finite total

questions.explanation: Direct comparison needs an upper bound whose own integral is known to be finite. For x at least 1, one over x squared is no larger than one over x to the three halves power, and that comparison integral is finite because its exponent exceeds 1, so the original total is finite as well. An integrand merely approaching zero proves nothing about the sum, since tiny terms can still accumulate, which is exactly what the harmonic series shows.
questions.hint: Find a decaying function no smaller than the integrand and whose total you already know.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: predict the sign change caused by reversing integration bounds
questions.stem: A student needs the total from hour 3 back to hour 1 rather than forward through the same span. Which statement about the sign is correct?

options.text: Swapping the two limits multiplies the value by negative one, because the orientation reverses
Swapping the two limits leaves the value unchanged, because the same interval is covered
options.misconception: believes the order of the limits has no effect on a definite integral

options.text: Swapping the two limits doubles the value, because both intervals are then counted
options.misconception: believes reversed limits cause the interval to be counted twice

options.text: Swapping the two limits makes the value zero, because the endpoints cancel exactly
options.misconception: believes a reversed definite integral always vanishes by endpoint cancellation

questions.explanation: A definite integral is signed, and the sign records the direction in which the accumulation is taken. Traversing the same interval backwards accumulates the same magnitudes in the opposite sense, so the value changes sign while its size stays the same. This matches the evaluation formula, in which the antiderivative is taken at the upper limit first, so exchanging the limits reverses the subtraction.
questions.hint: Compare the evaluation formula before and after exchanging the two limits.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a definite integral of a monomial
questions.stem: A strength model integrates five times the fourth power of x from 0 to 2. What is that definite integral? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The power rule turns the integrand into x to the fifth power, whose value at 2 is 32 and whose value at 0 is 0, so the definite integral is 32. Dropping the factor 5 on the way would give 32 over 5, and reading the value at 0 as 5 would inject a spurious term that the lower limit is supposed to kill.
questions.hint: Integrate the monomial first, then evaluate at both limits.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: carry out one round of integration by parts and read off a coefficient
questions.stem: A chemist integrates the product of x and e to the x by parts, taking the polynomial factor as the one to differentiate. First state the matching integral of the exponential factor, then report the coefficient of x inside the parentheses of the answer.

options.misconception: believes the leftover subtraction also flips the sign of the linear term
believes the coefficient of x doubles when the integrand is linear rather than quadratic
believes the tabular pattern for a quadratic integrand applies to a linear one

questions.explanation: With the polynomial differentiated and the exponential integrated, the first round leaves the exponential of x times the quantity x minus 1, and the leftover integral is the integral of one, so nothing further remains. The coefficient of x is therefore 1. Differentiating the result confirms it, since the exponential times the quantity x minus 1 plus the exponential reproduces x times the exponential exactly.
questions.hint: Carry out the single round of parts and then differentiate to check.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: identify the upper curve on an interval and compute the enclosed area
questions.stem: Two curves, y equal to the cube of x and y equal to the square of x, enclose a lens between x equal to 1 and x equal to 2. First state which curve is on top there, then report the enclosed area as a fraction.

options.text: The cube is on top, giving an area of seventeen twelfths
The square is on top, giving an area of seventeen twelfths
options.misconception: believes the smaller power is the upper curve on this interval

options.text: The cube is on top, giving an area of four thirds
options.misconception: believes integrating the upper curve alone gives the enclosed area

options.text: The curves cross inside the interval, so the area there is zero
options.misconception: believes the two curves coincide somewhere between 1 and 2

questions.explanation: For x above 1 the cube of x exceeds the square of x, so the cube is the upper curve and the area is the integral of the difference. That antiderivative is x to the fourth over 4 minus x cubed over 3, which gives seventeen twelfths over the interval. The curves meet only at 0 and 1, so nothing crosses inside this interval, and four thirds is the upper curve integrated on its own.
questions.hint: Compare the two powers at a sample point above 1, then integrate the difference.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: rewrite an improper integral as a limit and evaluate it
questions.stem: An improper integral runs from 1 out to infinity with integrand one over the cube of x. First rewrite it as a limit of proper integrals, then report the value it converges to.

options.text: 0.5, because the tail beyond the bound shrinks like one half over the squared bound
1, because the exponent 3 clears the denominator exactly once
options.misconception: believes the integral of any power greater than one equals one

options.text: infinity, because the integrand never reaches zero at a finite point
options.misconception: believes a total is infinite whenever the integrand is never zero

options.text: 0, because the integrand approaches zero as x grows past every bound
options.misconception: believes a vanishing integrand forces the total to vanish

questions.explanation: Truncating at a bound b and evaluating gives one half minus one half over b squared, and the second term vanishes as b grows, so the improper integral is one half. The convergence is exactly the p-type behaviour with exponent above 1. Reaching zero instead would confuse the integrand's limit with the total, and reaching infinity would confuse integrability with the size of the integrand.
questions.hint: Truncate at a finite bound, evaluate, and let the bound grow.
